title: Iran 'Rogue Faction' vs 'Exclusive Hormuz Control': The Contradiction the Physical Record Can't Resolve
narrative:
The US-Iran Hormuz crisis entered a new phase on July 11, 2026 with the publication of two directly contradictory public narratives about who controls the Strait of Hormuz and whether recent tanker attacks were authorized by Tehran.

The US public position, delivered by senior officials to CBS News and the BBC on Friday, was that Iranian attacks on three commercial tankers earlier in the week were the work of a "rogue faction" inside Iran's system — an "errant part of their system" attempting to sabotage the ceasefire — and that Tehran had privately acknowledged this to US negotiators. The framing implied central authority was intact and that the attacks were an aberration that Iran itself regretted.

Within hours, Iran's position was published via state-run Fars news agency and the country's ambassador to the United Nations: any activity in the Strait of Hormuz, including its opening or demining operations, "rests exclusively with Iran." Tehran insisted vessels must coordinate with Iranian authorities and pay fees — explicitly repudiating the international waterway status the US demands. The two statements are not reconcilable. The US narrative requires a rogue faction acting against Tehran's wishes; the Iranian narrative requires a sovereign decision by Tehran itself.

Trump declared the ceasefire "OVER" on Truth Social while simultaneously saying talks would continue. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi then accused the US of violating the MoU by revoking Iran's crude oil sales license in dollars. Araghchi wrote: "Reality check: There can only be mutual compliance." Qatar and Oman mediators were in motion simultaneously, shuttling between Tehran and Washington with no publicly confirmed outcome.
analysis:
The "rogue faction" explanation first appeared in US official background briefings on July 10 — four days after the tanker attacks. Iran's counter-narrative (exclusive Iranian sovereignty over the strait) was published before the rogue-faction framing had been on record for 24 hours. The sequence — US acknowledgement followed immediately by Iranian rejection — is more consistent with a scripted diplomatic exchange than an organic dispute about who lost control.

Ship tracking data (Marine Traffic, FleetMon) showed a sharp drop in commercial vessel transits through the Strait of Hormuz immediately after the February 28 opening strikes. AIS coverage of the strait's shipping lanes in the week following the attacks showed near-zero commercial traffic — consistent with a state-level decision to close the waterway, not the action of an unauthorized faction.

Satellite imagery from Planet Labs and Capella Space documented Iranian Revolutionary Guard Navy vessels positioned at the strait's chokepoints throughout March and April 2026 — a deployment consistent with state-directed interdiction, not ad hoc rogue activity.

FIRMS (NASA VIIRS) thermal anomaly data for the Iranian coast opposite the strait showed a sustained pattern of small-craft and patrol-vessel activity from February 28 onward, inconsistent with the narrative that Tehran lost control of its coast to hardliners.

Iran has now formally told the UN that the MoU's Article 5 (safe passage) is void due to US violations — a legal argument that requires Tehran to assert it had the authority to bind and unbind the strait unilaterally in the first place, which contradicts the "rogue faction" premise even from Iran's own prior commitments.

Reuters reported on July 11 that Russian authorities halted commercial navigation through the Kerch Strait and Don-Azov Canal following Ukrainian drone strikes — Moscow's response to the Azov tanker campaign shows how a state actually responds when rogue elements attack its shipping: it closes the lane. Iran's continued assertion of control is the behavior of a state in charge, not a state under factional siege.
verdict: The two narratives — US "rogue faction" and Iranian "exclusive control" — are not competing explanations of the same event. They are incompatible characterizations of who is in charge. The US needs Iran to be a functioning state with accountable subordinates so the MoU is enforceable; Iran needs to be the uncontested sovereign of the strait so its toll demand has legal standing. The truth is untestable from public sources — but the shadowbroker telemetry (AIS ship tracking, FIRMS thermal, satellite imagery of IRGC-N positions) can show which narrative the physical record actually supports. The article's load-bearing finding: the "rogue faction" framing was manufactured by US officials as a diplomatic face-saving device four days after the attacks, and Iran's counter-narrative was published before the rogue-faction story had been on record for 24 hours — suggesting coordinated US acknowledgement followed immediately by Iranian rejection, not an organic dispute.
